strengths: The part-centric assembly graph is an intuitive and potentially useful representation: naming interacting parts and oriented surfaces can remove ambiguities that object-level predicates such as “on” or “against” leave unresolved.

PARSE-10K is ambitious in scale, with 10,000 scenes, 132 object categories, part-segmented assets, dense arrangements, and part-level contact graphs. If released with the stated annotations, it could support several spatial-reasoning and generation tasks.

The work connects representation, procedural synthesis, VLM supervision, and scene generation in a coherent pipeline. The large reported improvements after fine-tuning Qwen3-VL suggest that the generated supervision contains learnable spatial information.

The manuscript is generally easy to follow, and the figures provide clear qualitative illustrations of PAGs, constraint-driven placement, and generated scenes. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/9e68e9cc60a04e3e8c557674b4cafd5c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The central technical claims are insufficiently validated. There is no quantitative evaluation of the solver’s relation-satisfaction rate, collision rate, post-simulation stability, failure rate, runtime, or advantage over an object-level solver. Thus claims of efficient search, guaranteed constraint satisfaction, and physically valid synthesis are not established empirically.

The solver is described only conceptually. The paper provides no mathematical definition of the feasible sets or individual constraints, algorithm or pseudocode, tolerance choices, handling of mutually inconsistent relations, asset-selection procedure, or recovery from failed placement. A DAG and unique supporter provide an assembly order but do not by themselves guarantee geometric feasibility or physical stability; they also exclude common multi-support configurations. Physics simulation may alter previously satisfied relations, but post-simulation compliance is not measured.

Dataset construction is substantially under-specified. The manuscript does not explain how PAGs are extracted from real images, how much manual intervention is required, how assets from heterogeneous sources are normalized and assigned canonical part surfaces, or how annotation accuracy is audited. Defining contacts solely by part proximity of at most 1 mm can confuse near-contact with load-bearing contact. Table 1 also mixes or insufficiently defines object/asset counts and average scene counts, making the comparison difficult to interpret.

The VLM evidence is vulnerable to synthetic-domain and template shortcuts. Dataset sizes, train/validation/test splits, scene and asset disjointness, question counts, class balance, and per-relation results are absent. Randomly substituted MCQ distractors may be implausible and easy to reject without genuine spatial understanding. The unspecified number of manually labeled COCO images is mixed into evaluation without a separate real-image result, so the claimed generalization to real imagery is unsupported.

The large fine-tuning gains compare an in-domain trained model against zero-shot general-purpose models. There is no size-matched object-level supervision baseline, synthetic-data baseline without PAG annotations, or ablation separating part-level supervision from rendering volume and task-specific output training. Consequently, the results do not isolate the value of the proposed representation.

The scene-generation comparison is confounded: InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT, whereas the proposed architecture is trained on PARSE-10K, whose scenes have far more objects. No baseline is retrained on PARSE-10K and no proposed model is trained on 3D-FRONT. The 20-person, 12-scene user study lacks uncertainty estimates, significance tests, selection/randomization details, and objective metrics for collision, stability, contact fidelity, or PAG compliance. The realism preference is only 38.8% versus 33.8%, making the manuscript’s broad realism claim too strong.

Reproducibility is weak in the provided manuscript: it delegates unspecified hyperparameters to a supplement that is not present and gives no data/code link, split specification, model size, training budget, prompting protocol, or API settings. These are material omissions rather than presentation-only refinements.

strengths: The central idea—representing support, contact, containment, and alignment at the level of object parts and oriented surfaces—is well motivated. PAG provides a useful bridge between semantic scene graphs and geometric constraints.
PARSE-10K could be a valuable resource: its claimed scale, part-segmented assets, densely populated scenes, and part-level contact graphs address a gap in existing indoor-scene datasets.

The paper explores two relevant applications. In particular, the substantial improvement of the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL over its unfine-tuned counterpart suggests that the synthetic supervision is learnable and potentially useful.
The manuscript is visually clear, and Figures 2–4 effectively communicate the representation, intended solver behavior, and fine-grained control.
weaknesses: The construction of the dataset’s crucial input—the PAGs derived from “real-image layout priors”—is essentially unspecified. The paper does not explain the image source, relation-extraction process, amount of manual annotation, quality control, annotation reliability, or duplicate handling. This is a material reproducibility gap, especially because the conclusion acknowledges that PAG construction is partially manual.

The solver is described only conceptually. The manuscript lacks precise definitions of pose variables, constraint functions, feasible-set computation, surface extraction, sampling, collision resolution, failure handling, and computational cost. Moreover, a DAG and unique-supporter assumption do not by themselves guarantee constraint consistency, stability, non-collision, or physical realizability, contrary to the paper’s strong language.

Physical-validity claims are not quantitatively substantiated. The SAPIEN refinement lacks simulation parameters and stability criteria, while defining contacts as part pairs within 1 mm does not establish force-bearing physical contact. No collision rate, stability measurement, constraint-satisfaction rate, solver success rate, or comparison against an object-level solver is reported.

The VLM experiments omit essential details, including dataset and split sizes, numbers of views and questions, class balance, prompts, decoding settings, IoU threshold, synonym-normalization rules, and fine-tuning configuration. Possible leakage through shared assets, layouts, or PAG templates is not addressed.

Table 2 primarily compares an in-domain fine-tuned model with zero-shot general-purpose VLMs. This demonstrates in-domain adaptation but does not establish broad improvement in spatial understanding. Randomly replaced MCQ distractors may be implausible or easy, and there is no matched fine-tuning baseline, external benchmark, or ablation isolating the effect of part-level supervision. The unspecified COCO subset is not reported separately despite being presented as evidence of generalization.

The scene-generation comparison is confounded: InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT, whereas the proposed variants use PARSE-10K, so architecture, data distribution, object count, and conditioning are not controlled. No automated measures of relation satisfaction, collision, stability, fidelity, or diversity are provided.

The user study is too limited to support claims of substantially improved realism. It involves only 20 participants and 12 scenes per participant, with no description of randomization, pairing, scene sampling, inter-rater agreement, confidence intervals, or significance testing. The realism preference is only 38.8% versus 33.8% for InstructScene, and the unconditioned variant performs worse than InstructScene on both realism and contact fidelity.

Table 1 contains apparent numerical or labeling inconsistencies. For example, 18,656 objects across 211 HSSD scenes does not equal 329.7 objects per scene, and 13,151 objects across 18,968 3D-FRONT scenes does not equal 6.9. For PARSE-10K, 17,372 appears to denote reusable assets, whereas 49.9 placed objects per scene implies about 499,000 instances. This weakens the comparative dataset evidence.

Key ablations are absent, including object-level versus part-level constraints, explicit versus inferred surfaces, physics refinement, real-image priors, asset-source composition, and sensitivity to canonical-pose and oblique-contact errors. The part-centric direction has merit, but under-specification of the core pipeline and inadequate validation of physical correctness and generalization are consequential scientific weaknesses, making weak rejection appropriate.

strengths: The central idea is well motivated and reasonably original: modeling relations between specific object parts and oriented surfaces addresses genuine ambiguities in object-level scene graphs and linguistic prepositions.
The Part-centric Assembly Graph and coarse-to-fine solver form a coherent framework connecting representation, constrained 3D assembly, physics refinement, dataset creation, and downstream learning.

PARSE-10K is potentially valuable: it reportedly contains 10,000 scenes across 17 room types, 132 object categories, 17,372 part-segmented assets, dense contacts, and an average of 49.9 instantiated objects per scene—an unusual combination of scale and part-level structure.

The downstream evidence is promising. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL raises visual-relation accuracy from 86.2% to 97.4%, part-contact accuracy from 60.4% to 86.2%, and grounded scene-graph F1 from 33.2% to 76.6%. Reporting both bounding-box-dependent and grounding-agnostic SGG metrics is informative.

The conditioned generation variant receives the most user-study votes for complexity, realism, and contact fidelity. The manuscript is visually clear, and its figures communicate PAG structure and controllability effectively. weaknesses: The most material weakness is insufficient direct validation of the framework's physical and geometric claims. The paper gives no constraint-satisfaction rate, collision or penetration metric, post-simulation stability measure, contact-annotation accuracy, solver runtime, or failure rate. A DAG and unique-supporter assumption provide an assembly order but do not by themselves guarantee physical realizability, contrary to some of the manuscript's wording.

Dataset construction and quality control are under-specified. The manuscript does not adequately explain how real-image layout priors become PAGs, how much manual intervention is required, how part labels and canonical frames are harmonized across source datasets and generated assets, or how train/validation/test leakage is prevented.

The VLM evaluation is largely conducted on a benchmark generated from the same synthetic pipeline used for fine-tuning. The real-image test is described only as “some” manually labeled COCO images, without its size, composition, or separate results. Thus, the strong aggregate gains do not establish real-domain generalization.

The evaluation lacks sample counts, confidence intervals, variance across runs, and relevant ablations. In particular, it does not isolate the contributions of part-level edges, object-level edges, physics refinement, real-image priors, or dataset scale. Randomly substituted MCQ distractors may also permit shortcut-based performance.

The scene-generation comparison is confounded: InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT, whereas the proposed architecture is trained on PARSE-10K. Consequently, differences cannot be cleanly attributed to the dataset, PAG conditioning, or architecture. Automated metrics for relation compliance, collision, stability, diversity, and contact fidelity are absent.

The user study is small and incompletely specified: 20 participants each assess 12 scenes, but the manuscript does not state the number of comparisons per method, pairing and randomization procedure, participant expertise, rating interface, significance tests, or inter-rater agreement. Moreover, the unconditioned model is worse than InstructScene for realism and contact fidelity, while the conditioned gains on realism are modest.

Table 1 is internally unclear. The reported “# Objects” values appear to denote unique assets rather than scene instances, yet the column is compared with average objects per scene; several ratios are inconsistent—for example, 18,656 divided by 211 is not 329.7. This weakens the claimed dataset comparison and should be corrected.

Reproducibility is presently limited: despite saying that PARSE-10K is released, the manuscript provides no visible access link, license, data format specification, split definition, solver pseudocode, or sufficient training and optimization details in the provided document. These reservations are meaningful, but the representation, dataset scale, and large downstream improvements still make the supported contribution lean toward acceptance.

strengths: The central idea is useful and relevant: representing support, containment, and contact between named object parts can resolve ambiguities that object-level scene graphs cannot, while providing explicit control for scene synthesis.

PARSE combines a concrete representation, a coarse-to-fine constraint solver, physics simulation, and a sizable derived resource. PARSE-10K contains 10,000 scenes, 132 categories, 17,372 part-segmented assets, and an average of 49.9 objects per scene, making it potentially valuable for contact-rich spatial reasoning.

The manuscript explains the graph structure, relation vocabulary, geometric constraints, simulation procedure, contact extraction, and downstream architectures reasonably clearly. The appendix provides useful implementation details, including optimizer settings and simulation parameters.

The reported downstream gains are large: the fine-tuned Qwen3-VL model improves over its base model on all three reasoning tasks, and the conditioned generator receives the highest user preference for realism and contact fidelity. These results suggest that the proposed supervision contains a meaningful signal.
weaknesses: The main physical-validity claims are not adequately verified. A DAG and unique supporter provide an assembly order but do not ensure geometric feasibility or physical realizability. The algorithm explicitly permits failed placements and uses rejection sampling, yet the paper reports no placement success rate, failure rate, runtime, rejection count, post-simulation relation-retention rate, collision rate, or stability metric. Thus claims of efficient generation and physically consistent scenes lack direct quantitative support.

Dataset diversity is overstated or insufficiently analyzed. The 10,000 scenes originate from only 200 manually designed PAGs, apparently with asset and scale resampling. The paper provides no graph-level diversity statistics or comparison against template diversity in prior datasets. Moreover, the claimed extraction of real-image layout priors is described in the appendix as manually designing PAGs merely inspired by images, which is materially different from an automated extraction pipeline.

The VLM evaluation has serious leakage and fairness ambiguities. Splits are disjoint only at the generated-scene level, not at the underlying 200-PAG template level, so near-identical structures may occur across training and test sets. Test-set sizes, class distributions, sampling ratios, IoU thresholds, synonym-normalization rules, and the number and results of COCO examples are not reported. Random label replacement can create easy or implausible MCQ distractors, while part contacts derived in 3D may not be visually observable from a rendered view. Comparing a task-fine-tuned model against zero-shot general-purpose models therefore does not establish broad spatial-reasoning generalization.

The scene-generation evidence is heavily confounded. InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT while the proposed model is trained on PARSE-10K, so architecture, training data, object count, and scene distribution vary simultaneously. There is no same-data baseline, no object-level versus part-level conditioning ablation, and no objective measurement of relation satisfaction, penetration, support, stability, diversity, or contact accuracy. The 20-person, 12-scene user study is small and lacks uncertainty, significance testing, randomization details, and agreement statistics.

The part-contact annotations are not validated. Contacts are inferred by sampled-point proximity between convex-decomposition hulls and then mapped to the nearest visual-mesh parts; this can introduce false contacts or miss thin/local contacts. No manually annotated audit or precision/recall study supports the claim that these are high-quality dense annotations.

The solver itself is only partially specified and lacks comparative evidence. Surface proxies may fall back to bounding-box faces, thresholds and trial limits are mostly unspecified, no backtracking is described when early asset or pose choices make later constraints infeasible, and there is no comparison with an object-centric solver to demonstrate the claimed search-space or efficiency advantage.

Some dataset statistics are internally unclear. For example, Table 1 reports 18,656 objects and 211 HSSD scenes but an average of 329.7 objects per scene, which does not follow from those counts; analogous inconsistencies occur for other rows, suggesting that unique assets and object instances may be conflated. Data/code release details and licensing for Internet-derived, generated, and aggregated assets are also absent. These reproducibility concerns are material, whereas minor typographical and wording issues are merely presentational.

strengths: The manuscript :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/d74bb73531354ff49fad4aa6cdccb832/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"} addresses an important limitation of object-level scene graphs: many support and contact relationships are naturally defined between object parts. The proposed Part-centric Assembly Graph is intuitive and potentially useful for controllable scene synthesis and spatial reasoning.

PARSE-10K is ambitious in scale, with 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories, dense object arrangements, and part-level contact graphs. If released with suitable licensing and quality control, it could be a valuable resource.

The coarse-to-fine solver provides a sensible procedural framework: object-level constraints narrow placement regions, part-level surface constraints refine poses, collision checks reject invalid samples, and physics simulation provides final refinement.

The paper considers two distinct downstream applications, and the reported improvements on its synthetic spatial-reasoning benchmark are large. The scene-level train/test split appropriately prevents leakage across camera views of the same scene.

The presentation is generally clear, the visual examples communicate the intended representation well, and the supplement provides useful asset-processing, contact-extraction, training, and architectural details.
weaknesses: The central physical-validity claims are not adequately established. A DAG and a unique supporter provide an assembly order but do not themselves ensure physical realizability, contrary to the manuscript's wording. The solver can encounter empty feasible sets or exhaust its trials and discard objects, yet no placement success rate, rejection rate, runtime, collision rate, stability measurement, or preservation of PAG relations after physics simulation is reported.

The solver is described only at a high level. Critical operations such as rotation solving, feasible-pose intersection, surface clipping, tolerances, thresholds, maximum trials, and failure handling are not specified sufficiently to verify the claimed guarantees. Axis-aligned directional surfaces derived from canonical bounding boxes are also a restrictive proxy for curved or irregular contacts, but their failure modes are not evaluated.

Dataset quality receives little empirical validation. Object density and the number of detected contacts demonstrate quantity, not correctness or realism. There is no human audit of part labels, contact precision/recall, penetration, post-simulation stability, or semantic plausibility. The proximity-based contact detector and nearest-part mapping can introduce both false contacts and incorrect part assignments without a reported accuracy study.

The claimed diversity is overstated relative to the construction process: 10,000 scenes are generated from only 200 manually designed PAGs described as being merely inspired by real images. The paper does not quantify graph-template diversity, asset reuse, near-duplicates, or train/test separation at the PAG-template level. Consequently, the downstream model may benefit from memorizing a small family of synthetic structures.

The VLM evaluation cannot support the broad generalization claims. Test-set sizes, class distributions, random baselines, sampling ratios, and the number of real COCO examples are omitted, and synthetic and real results are not reported separately. The phrase 'some manually labeled real images' is not reproducible evidence of real-domain transfer.

The VLM comparison is confounded: the proposed model is explicitly fine-tuned on the benchmark's rendering style, vocabulary, and output format, whereas the listed general-purpose models appear to be evaluated without comparable adaptation. Randomly constructed MCQ distractors may permit shortcuts. There is no ablation against fine-tuning Qwen3-VL on equivalent object-level supervision, no part-supervision ablation, and no cross-dataset spatial benchmark showing that part-level data is responsible for the gains.

The scene-generation evidence is particularly weak. The only external baseline is trained on a different dataset, while architecture, object density, inputs, and training distribution also differ. Thus the comparison does not isolate the benefit of PARSE-10K or PAG conditioning. No quantitative relation-satisfaction, collision, stability, contact, diversity, or distributional-fidelity metrics are provided.

The generation conclusions rely on a small user study of 20 participants and 12 scenes, with no confidence intervals, significance tests, randomization details, participant protocol, or per-scene analysis. 'Complexity' preference largely reflects the intentionally higher object count and is not evidence of realism. The conditioned model's realism preference is only 38.8%, making claims of substantially improved physical realism too strong.

Important ablations are absent: part-level versus object-level graphs, individual relation types, physics refinement, surface inference, PAG-template count, contact annotations, and sensitivity to canonical-pose or part-segmentation errors. These omissions prevent attribution of the reported improvements to the paper's central contribution.

Reproducibility remains uncertain because the manuscript does not clearly commit to releasing the dataset, code, assets, annotations, prompts, evaluation sets, or manual PAG templates. Several generated assets and internet reference images also raise unaddressed licensing questions. Overall, the representation and dataset concept have merit, but the missing validation and confounded downstream experiments materially weaken the scientific support, favoring weak rejection rather than rejection on presentation grounds alone.

strengths: The paper addresses an important gap between coarse object-level scene graphs and the part-specific contacts needed for physical scene reasoning. The PAG representation, constraint-based solver, and PARSE-10K dataset form a coherent contribution with clear potential for scene synthesis, embodied reasoning, and VLM training.

PARSE-10K is substantial in scale: 10,000 scenes, 17,372 part-segmented assets across 132 categories, an average of 49.9 objects per scene, and explicit part-level contact graphs. The visual examples show unusually dense and varied arrangements.

The solver is conceptually clear and interpretable. Separating coarse object-level localization from part-surface alignment provides fine-grained control, while the supplementary relation dictionary and algorithm make the main mechanics understandable.

The downstream results are promising. Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL raises visual-relation accuracy from 86.2% to 97.4%, part-contact accuracy from 60.4% to 86.2%, and grounded SGG F1 from 33.2% to 76.6%. PAG-conditioned generation also receives the most votes for realism and contact fidelity.
The manuscript is well organized and visually effective, with helpful diagrams, qualitative examples, implementation details, and an explicit limitations discussion.
weaknesses: The central claims of physical validity are not adequately quantified. The paper reports contact counts and a small perceptual study, but no collision rate, constraint-satisfaction rate, post-simulation displacement, stability/failure rate, penetration depth, or comparison of solver efficiency against object-level search. A DAG and unique-supporter assumption provide an assembly order but do not by themselves ensure physical realizability.

The evaluation split may substantially overestimate generalization. The 10,000 scenes originate from only 200 manually designed PAGs, yet the reported split is at the generated-scene level rather than the PAG-template level. Consequently, structurally near-identical PAGs can plausibly occur in training and testing. A held-out-PAG and preferably held-out-asset evaluation is needed to support the stated generalization claims.

The VLM evaluation is insufficiently specified: test-set sizes, task composition, answer balance, dataset mixing ratios, and the number and separate performance of manually labeled COCO images are absent. Randomly replacing labels to form MCQ distractors may also create easy negatives. Thus, the large gains convincingly show in-distribution adaptation but do not yet establish robust real-image or compositional generalization.

The scene-generation study confounds dataset, model, conditioning, and scene complexity: InstructScene is trained on 3D-FRONT, whereas the proposed model is trained on PARSE-10K. There is no controlled comparison on the same training data, no object-level-versus-part-level conditioning ablation, and no objective relation, collision, contact, or stability metrics. The user study includes only 20 participants and 12 scenes per participant, with no uncertainty or significance analysis.

Dataset quality is not directly validated. Part contacts are inferred through sampled near-contact points on convex hulls and then mapped to the nearest visual-mesh parts, but the paper provides no manual audit, precision/recall measurement, sensitivity to the 1 mm threshold, or analysis of how simulation changes intended PAG relations.

Table 1 appears internally inconsistent: for example, 18,656 objects across 211 HSSD scenes cannot yield the stated average of 329.7 objects per scene, and analogous inconsistencies occur for 3D-FRONT and FurniScene. The “# Objects” column may mean unique assets rather than placed instances, but this must be corrected because it affects the dataset comparison.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite useful appendix details. Important solver thresholds and maximum trials, PAG construction rules, failure statistics, evaluation-set sizes, prompt-generation details, and release information for the dataset, code, PAGs, and annotations are not specified. Overall, the representation and resource are promising, but the missing controlled and leakage-resistant evaluation keeps the evidence near the acceptance boundary.
